k-1.x_notes: Ten concrete problems with pictured piles; same core sequence as Y (choose 1st/2nd, cross out the winning take, shade 1-12 under {1,2}, beat greedy Ben, {1,2,3} and {1,3} tables, pile of 20 under three rules, two-pile pairs, list every game). All answers check: losing piles at multiples of 3, of 4, and the even piles; 20 gives 1st/2nd/2nd; pairs (2,2),(3,3),(1,4) are 2nd and (1,2) is 1st; Ben can be beaten at 3,4,6,7. Problem 1 uses piles 3-6, so it contains two losing piles (3 and 6), which hints at the repeat. Problems 9 and 10 each get a full-page board with generous spacing, and Problem 9 has one ringed example (2+2) to show how to record, which helps non-readers. Problem 10 adds 'star each game the first player wins' (4 of the 8 games), which ties the listing back to winning and losing. Header reads 'Grades K-1', matching the other bands. Weaknesses: Problem 8 repeats the last-counter rule, and it uses six pages.
k-1.y_notes: Nearly identical problems, also mathematically correct and concrete, and it ends with the same full set of ten problems, so it does not stop too early. Problem 1 uses piles 2-5, which contain only one losing pile, so it gives less to notice. Problems 9 and 10 share one page with narrower boards and no recording example, and enough rows (7 and 10 for 5 and 8 games). Problem 10 only asks for listing, with no link back to who wins. Header says 'K-1' while the other bands say 'Grades 2-3/4-5'. Five pages.
k-1.reason: The content is essentially the same, but X's pile choice in Problem 1, its modeled recording and larger boards for the game-listing problems, and the star question that links listing to winning make it slightly more usable and more mathematical for kindergartners.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strong, correct sequence: play {1,2} piles, test four plans against every reply (Mia and Ana always win, Leo can lose, and Sam's plan loses because his opening move is wrong), classify 1-20 under {1,3,4} (2nd at 2,7,9,14,16), extend to 25/30/37/50 (1st/2nd/2nd/1st), test Kai/Theo/Zoe (greedy Kai and copycat Theo can lose, Zoe always wins), compare {1,2,4} with {1,2} (Jon is wrong because both have losing piles at the multiples of 3), and two piles (5,5 is a mirroring win for the second player). Problem 5 adds 'if a plan wins every time, explain why it can never lose', which is exactly the outline's 'every reply' emphasis and matters for Zoe. Problem 6 says clearly what to record (shade the go-second piles for each rule) and asks why it holds beyond 15, with a large box to answer. Problem 7 gets its own page. Weakness: a little more 'explain' text.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Same problems and the same correct answers. The intro clarifies that each problem gives its own rule. Problem 5 drops the request to justify a plan that always wins, so Zoe's case can end at a circled guess. Problem 6 gives a blank two-row table with no instruction about what to write in the cells ('Check every starting pile'), no space to answer 'Is Jon right?', and no push to explain beyond 15, so the generalization is left out. Problem 7's explanation box is smaller. Five pages.
grades-2-3.reason: The packets are almost the same, but X's Problem 6 has a clear recording action and asks why the pattern continues past 15, and its Problem 5 asks children to justify a plan against every reply. Both are where the real thinking for this band happens.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Rich and correct throughout. {1,2} and {1,3,4} tables with explanations. Seven rules where the matching pairs are {1,2}/{1,2,4}, {1,3}/{1,3,5} and {1,4}/{1,4,6}, with numbers spaced well for circling. Greedy Kai under {1,3,4} errs at 5,8,10,12,15,17,19,22,24,26,29 and is never wrong for {1,3} or {1,3,5}, and X asks for an explanation. Problem 5's inverse lists are all new and contrast well: multiples of 5 gives {1,2,3,4}, {2,8,10,...} needs a real search ({1,4,5}), {3,7,10,...} gives {1,2,6}, and {3,5,8,...} is impossible, which needs a proof. {1,6,9} shows a preperiod (the repeat starts at 10) and leads to the pigeonhole argument before the two-pile work. Problem 8 asks for the losing pairs of different sizes ((0,2),(0,7),(1,3),(4,6),...), and Problem 9 asks explicitly how the mex labels (period 0,1,0,1,2,3,2) explain the Problem 8 grid before applying them to 11 & 13 (losing) and 12 & 18 (winning). The single-pile, then two-pile, then labels sequence is coherent.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Same core and the same correct answers. Problem 3's 24-cell rows are cramped for circling. Problem 4 has more precise wording but no explanation. In Problem 5, two of the four lists (4,8,12,... and 2,5,7,10,...) are just {1,2,3} and {1,4} from Problem 3, so they become lookups. The {1,3,4} two-pile grid has no follow-up, and the label problem never asks how the numbers relate to the grid, so the key Sprague-Grundy discovery is left implicit before the 11/13 and 12/18 questions. {1,6,9} and the periodicity proof come last, after the two-pile work, which makes the order less coherent. There is ample work for 40 minutes either way.
grades-4-5.reason: X's inverse-problem lists are all genuine challenges, and it explicitly links the mex labels to the two-pile grid, so the hardest idea is built up, not left implicit. Y would need edits to Problems 5, 7 and 8 to match.

overall.reason: The two packets share nearly all their problems and both are mathematically correct, but X is consistently a little better in every band. It has better pile choices and recording models for K-1, asks for the generalization and the every-reply justification in 2-3, and has richer inverse problems and an explicit route to Sprague-Grundy values in 4-5. Y has no offsetting advantage, so the organizer would spend his editing time restoring what X already has.
